1.pericope_label: To his anointed, to Cyrus: the gates opened and the two leaved doors

schools.summary: Take the title as the ordinary one of kings by God's grace, note that it had not yet narrowed to its later sense, distinguish palace doors from city gates, and allow the ungirding to mean either weakening or disarming.
Feel the scandal of a heathen idolater called Messiah and answer it by making the title an office held for a season, and prefer the belt of royalty to the sinews because a promise to gird follows.
Render the verb simply as ungird, and furnish the prophecy from Herodotus, the hundred brazen gates and the river channel left open on the night of the feast.
Supply the disputed history from the pagan writers, refuse to read the promotion as praise of the man, and draw the maxim that God rarely trusts his own people with the world's wealth and power.

debates.question: In what sense is a heathen king called the LORD's anointed?

positions.view: in the ordinary sense the word then bore, a king by the grace of God as David was, before it narrowed to its later application
truly anointed though without material oil, since appointment and fitness for the office make the anointing
granted the title for a season only, because he discharged for a time the work of a redeemer, though he never forsook his superstitions

debates.question: What is meant by loosing the loins of kings?

positions.view: the belt of royalty, the badge of authority, since a promise to gird follows a few verses on and the contrast should stand
either a general figure of weakening or a specific one of disarming, the sword being hung from the girdle
both dignity and vigour, with the letter of it fulfilled in Belshazzar, whose joints were loosed at the writing on the wall
simply ungird, with no further gloss

debates.question: How should the crooked places be read?

positions.view: as mountains, following the Greek against a word hard to account for, with two manuscripts in support
as dwelling places made smooth, that is, obstacles removed
as hilly ground levelled, the work of pioneers before an army
as nothing new, the verse promising only an easy and rapid march under divine conduct

outliers.reading: Alone weighs the man's character against his commission, setting Xenophon's model prince beside the historians who call him haughty, cruel and bloodthirsty, and concludes that the preference was for Jacob's sake and not for his own.

themes: Thus saith the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him; and I will loose the loins of kings, to open before him the two leaved gates; and the gates shall not be shut;
I will go before thee, and make the crooked places straight: I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron:

3.pericope_label: Treasures of darkness: for Jacob my servant, that they may know from the rising of the sun

schools.summary: Refuse the legends and account for the treasure from the wealth of the city and the fall of Sardis, press the words servant and chosen for the ideal people, and read the girding as the reversal of the earlier ungirding.

Report the rabbinic tale of the sunken hoard and then count Pliny's figures, and hear God addressing the prince coldly, since the regard is for his own people and the word servant rests on free choice.

Convert the plunder into sterling and question the weight of the great cup, offer buried house floors as the plainer cause of the darkness, and list the three proofs by which all nations were to know.
Hear the bare declaration that there is none else as aimed at two dangers at once, the idolatry the prince inherited and the habit of universal monarchs of accepting worship themselves.

debates.question: Why are the treasures called treasures of darkness?

positions.view: because a former king sank his hoard in the bed of the river and it was revealed on the day the temple was ordered rebuilt
because householders buried coin beneath their floors for fear of thieves
because such things had long lain secret, with no further explanation offered
because the wealth of the city and the spoil of Sardis had been heaped up out of sight, no legend being needed

debates.question: For whose sake was the conqueror raised and named?

positions.view: for the ideal people, the true assembly rather than the nation in its outward standing, world history being ordered with a view to it
for the elect, the named deliverer standing as a figure of one called later for their sake
for God's own people and not for the prince, who is told as much plainly so that he may treat them kindly
for the redemption of Israel and the conversion of the heathen together, the one commission serving both

debates.question: When and how was the knowledge from sunrise to sunset fulfilled?

positions.view: not at once, since few then saw whose hand it was, but by report passed from neighbour to neighbour and fixed in lasting records
by three means together, the foretelling long before, the success given, and the overruling of a pagan heart
by the reach of the merism itself, since the east-west axis takes in the inhabited world as north and south do not

outliers.reading: Alone leaves the chapter to retell at length what Josephus reports of Alexander before Jerusalem, the tribute refused, the high priest going out in his robes, and the conqueror dismounting to prostrate himself, as evidence that the church is preserved by strange and unusual methods.
Alone suggests that the habit of universal monarchs of setting themselves up as gods accounts for no small part of how idolatry began, and reads the declaration as forestalling it.

themes: And I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that thou mayest know that I, the Lord, which call thee by thy name, am the God of Israel.
For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me.
I am the Lord, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:
That they may know from the rising of the sun, and from the west, that there is none beside me. I am the Lord, and there is none else.

7.pericope_label: I form the light and create darkness: drop down ye heavens, and woe to him that striveth

schools.summary: Rule the words out of the problem of the origin of evil, since what stands opposed to peace is suffering and not sin, and prefer the abrupt clause without supplied verbs, a potsherd among potsherds.

Settle the created evil from the shape of the sentence, peace being set opposite affliction and not righteousness, and hold the double front against those who make God the author of guilt and those who exempt him when the stroke falls by human hands.

Aim the declaration at Persian dualism by name, dating the doctrine early from Xenophon, and hear the potter's question as forestalling countrymen who resented rescue promised rather than captivity spared.

debates.question: What is the evil that is created?

positions.view: war and its miseries specifically, since as darkness is the privation of light, war is the privation of peace
suffering and not sin, the words bearing nothing on the insoluble problem of the origin of evil
adverse events of every kind, the contrast with peace settling it, so that God authors the evil of punishment and not of guilt
every register at once, from natural darkness and the eclipse to blindness, hardening and the last punishment

debates.question: Is the call for the heavens to drop down righteousness a prayer or a command?

positions.view: a command, God still speaking and ordering heaven and earth into service, the imperative being the ordinary prophetic one that stands for a future
not a petition of prophet or church but a promise and prophecy, though some heard in it an address to the angels
a vision of a new heaven and earth in which righteousness is at once the rain from one and the crop of the other
a passage imitated by a psalm of the restoration, whose blessings cannot be mere consequences of a return from exile

debates.question: Who is warned off by the woe on him that strives with his Maker?

positions.view: countrymen who resented being promised rescue rather than spared the captivity, with the Babylonian king who drank from the temple vessels also named
the impatient under delay, the flesh asking why the rescue is not quicker
any who would hinder the appointed man
the faint-hearted who complain of the divine ways, as an earlier chapter also opens
those who quarrel with the purposes and dispensations of God, and in the end with the author of righteousness himself

outliers.reading: Alone dates Persian dualism early enough to be the target here from an anecdote in Xenophon, where an officer who has threatened a captive he loves excuses himself by claiming two souls, a philosophy learned from that wicked sophist, Love.
Alone divides the two questions into distinct kinds of presumption, the first merely querying the work, the second declaring the workman handless.

themes: I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the Lord do all these things.

Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness: let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together; I the Lord have created it.
Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands?
Woe unto him that saith unto his father, What begettest thou? or to the woman, What hast thou brought forth?

11.pericope_label: Ask me of things to come: I have raised him up in righteousness, not for price nor reward

schools.summary: Concede that the received text invites consultation but judge an emendation more coherent, so that asking and commanding become the murmurers' own presumption answered by the results.
Keep the sentence whole as the application of the father and the potter, refuse two rival constructions, and make the raising up in righteousness a matter of fidelity rather than of punishment.
Repoint the verb on the Chaldee and the Greek so the clause reads as two indignant questions, and gloss the righteousness as justice done on Babylon and on the oppressed cause.
Take the received text as an invitation, distinguishing prescription from petition, and report the interrogative construction fairly without adopting it.

debates.question: Is the clause about asking and commanding an invitation or a rebuke?

positions.view: a rebuke, recovered by dropping a letter from the participle and taking the Chaldee verb with its interrogative prefix
a rebuke on a slight alteration of the text, more coherent with the context, though the received text says the opposite
a rebuke without emendation, the sentence continuing the figures of father and potter
an invitation, to consult the word and to seek by prayer, the imperious verb meaning petition and not prescription

debates.question: What does raised him up in righteousness mean?

positions.view: most justly, to punish the Babylonians and plead the cause of the oppressed
in pursuance of promises and to plead an injured cause together
fidelity, neither the punitive sense nor a promise that the man would reign justly, since God displays his rectitude chiefly in saving his people
the answer to the murmurers, proved by the city rebuilt and the exiles restored, owing nothing to a conqueror's usual greed

debates.question: Who is chiefly meant by the man raised up?

positions.view: the Persian and what he did for the Jews, evidently and without extension
the Persian in some respect but chiefly Christ, of whom he was a type

outliers.reading: Alone argues from the less to the greater out of the creation clause, that a providence governing the whole world must take peculiar care of a household, and brings in the sparrow that does not fall unpermitted.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, and his Maker, Ask me of things to come concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands command ye me.
I have made the earth, and created man upon it: I, even my hands, have stretched out the heavens, and all their host have I commanded.
I have raised him up in righteousness, and I will direct all his ways: he shall build my city, and he shall let go my captives, not for price nor reward, saith the Lord of hosts.

14.pericope_label: The labour of Egypt: verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, and Israel saved for ever

schools.summary: Measure the advance on the earlier ransom, distinguish what each nation brings, assign the exclamation to the church rather than the heathen, and read the hiding as the long appearance of negligence during the exile.

Find a first instalment in the tribute out of which the temple was rebuilt, guard the church's ascribed rule as her Head's sceptre, and reject both the hiding from the nations and the hiding of divinity under flesh.
Read the wealth and the willing captives as verified twice over, and take the hiding as a present concealment from the nations while Israel is saved and the counsels stay past finding out.

debates.question: Whose voice says, Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself?

positions.view: the church answering the confession of the heathen, the prophet lending his mouth to her amazement
either the wondering homage of the heathen continued or the prophet alone surveying unsearchable ways, both being possible
the prophet, contemplating the dispensations of God
the prophet reporting his own experience, or rather the church reporting hers

debates.question: In what sense does God hide himself?

positions.view: from the nations of the world at present, while he reveals himself to Israel and saves them
in his nature and essence, invisible and unsearchable in judgment, though he also withdraws from his own at times
in the withholding of help, not in essence, as the epithet Saviour standing beside it shows
in guiding the history of nations by secret ways that human eyes cannot discern
in seeming through the long exile to be negligent or unable, until it was seen that the Strong one had worked throughout

debates.question: What do the nations bring, and in what spirit?

positions.view: produce from two of them and labour itself from the third, who are strong but not wealthy, all coming as proselytes in self-imposed bondage
tribute from countries under Persian rule, out of which the temple was rebuilt, a literal first instalment of a larger homage
wealth gotten by their labour, brought to a rebuilt city, the captives willingly submitting

outliers.reading: Alone observes that the turn from adoration to the shaming of idol-makers changes not only the sentiment but the metre, the lines running out from the usual short measure into two long distichs.
Alone presses the noun rendered salvation, arguing that it means not rescue but removal into a wide place, that is into freedom and gladness, and disputes the dating of the plural for eternities.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, The labour of Egypt, and merchandise of Ethiopia and of the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over unto thee, and they shall be thine: they shall come after thee; in chains they shall come over, and they shall fall down unto thee, they shall make supplication unto thee, saying, Surely God is in thee; and there is none else, there is no God.
Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour.
They shall be ashamed, and also confounded, all of them: they shall go to confusion together that are makers of idols.
But Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end.

18.pericope_label: He created it not in vain: I have not spoken in secret, and the escaped of the nations assemble

schools.summary: Take the establishing as preparation for habitation, set the openness of the speaking against the hidden God of the earlier exclamation, and read the escaped as a fulness of the nations drawn out of the whole mass.

Reject the reading that narrows the earth to Judea, argue from the ground given for men's dwelling to the ground given for a church, defend the clarity of the written word, and make the escaped a remnant of grace.
Document the caverns and the ambiguous answers of the heathen oracles at length, prefix a causal particle from an old manuscript, and contrast the muttering from dens with a law given audibly.
Summon the actual refugees to hear the case against idols, that wood overlaid with gold can neither hear nor help, so that the old womb of idolatry might become its grave.

debates.question: What follows from the earth being formed to be inhabited?

positions.view: that it was not a chaos but the scene of human action, prepared for habitation
that it was made all the more surely to house a church, so that as long as the earth lasts the church lasts with it
that the maker of heaven and earth is the Saviour who speaks, distinguished from gods who made nothing

debates.question: Is the denial of speaking in secret aimed at the heathen oracles?

positions.view: yes, and at length, from the Sibyl's cave and the hollow at Delphi to the ambiguous answer that ruined the king who trusted it
yes, against the muttering out of the belly and from dens, answered by a law given audibly before a whole people
an allusion that appears likely, though the point being made is the clarity and certainty of the written word
aimed rather at the hidden God of the earlier exclamation, the revealing having gone on in the daylight of history and in the law written on men's hearts

debates.question: Who are the escaped of the nations that are summoned?

positions.view: the refugees actually released, Jews and others alike, called to hear the case against idolatry
not those who escaped the sword nor the Jews out of Babylon, but the Gentile remnant according to the election of grace
a fulness of the nations, a remnant drawn out of the whole mass of the heathen

outliers.reading: Alone extends the decree that the earth be inhabited to the maintenance of states and settled orders among barbarians and unbelievers, and to God's bearing with crimes that would otherwise have ended the race.

themes: For thus saith the Lord that created the heavens; God himself that formed the earth and made it; he hath established it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited: I am the Lord; and there is none else.
I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth: I said not unto the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain: I the Lord speak righteousness, I declare things that are right.
Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, ye that are escaped of the nations: they have no knowledge that set up the wood of their graven image, and pray unto a god that cannot save.

21.pericope_label: Look unto me and be ye saved: unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear

schools.summary: Rest the universal invitation on the joining of justice and salvation, parse the two imperatives as exhortation and promise, and find in the closing phrase the germ of the later thought of union.

Read the summons as the wall coming down and the refusal of it as insincerity rather than ignorance, insist that outward profession cannot be severed from the heart, and answer the objection that the ancient choice has failed.

Prefer an old manuscript's let them come together by appointment, report the Targum's Word as the object of the looking, and read the word that will not return as an ambassador who comes home with nothing done.

debates.question: Who speaks the confession about righteousness and strength?

positions.view: probably the Persian himself, whose decree acknowledged that the kingdoms had been given him
a speaker in a far-off time, whose confession the prophet overhears
every convert brought to submit, declaring a righteousness not inherent but received
believers who submit, in contrast with rebels who go on resisting, commentators being divided here
those whose bending of the knee is homage sworn and not forced

debates.question: How far has the universal bowing of the knee been accomplished?

positions.view: wherever the preaching is obeyed, but far from fully, since many still resist, which is why the apostle carries it forward to the judgment
in the faith of one people becoming the religion of mankind, that people keeping its distinct nationality
in a will that desires the conversion of all and their salvation through it, and will not rest till it has its object
in the coming of all nations, not the Jews only, as the prediction of a universal spread already discerned by the Targum

outliers.reading: Alone turns the oath into a rule about swearing, that since all confirmation of truth belongs to God no name of saint or creature may be mixed into a sworn appeal, and alone answers the objection that calling the nations would void the promise made to the fathers.
Alone works the imperative pastorally into a list of what must be looked away from before it can be obeyed, idols and creatures, one's own doings and tears, and even one's own graces.

themes: Tell ye, and bring them near; yea, let them take counsel together: who hath declared this from ancient time? who hath told it from that time? have not I the Lord? and there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Saviour; there is none beside me.
Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.
I have sworn by myself, the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return, That unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.
Surely, shall one say, in the Lord have I righteousness and strength: even to him shall men come; and all that are incensed against him shall be ashamed.
In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory.
